items.q: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) assigns…
choices: Unique sequential numbers restarting at 1 inside each department
Ranks that skip numbers on ties
The department's total salary to every row
items.explain: ROW_NUMBER is unique and sequential within each partition; RANK is the one that ties and skips.

items.q: An append-only incremental load double-counts revenue the moment…
choices: Source rows can be updated after they were first loaded
The load runs on a schedule
The extract is full, not incremental
items.explain: Appends assume immutability. If source rows change after loading, you need upserts or watermark logic — the classic incremental-load trap.

items.q: Data skew in Spark means…
choices: One partition holds far more data than the rest, stalling the job
Data is perfectly balanced across partitions
The cluster has too many nodes
items.explain: Skew: a hot key lands most rows on one partition, so one task runs long while the rest idle — the first scaling question in DE interviews.

items.q: Exactly-once processing in a streaming pipeline realistically requires…
choices: Idempotent sinks combined with transactional offsets or framework support
items.explain: Exactly-once is a system property: the source offsets and the sink writes must commit atomically, or sinks must tolerate replays idempotently.

items.q: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension…
choices: Preserves history by inserting new rows with effective dates
Overwrites the old value in place
items.explain: Type 2 keeps every version as a new row (effective/expiry dates); Type 1 overwrites. Interviewers ask which you chose and why.

items.q: Event time matters separately from processing time because…
choices: Late or out-of-order events land in the wrong window if you use arrival time
items.explain: Using arrival time assigns events to windows by when they showed up, not when they happened — watermarks exist to bound that lateness.

items.q: An idempotent pipeline is one where…
choices: Rerunning it produces the same result with no duplicates
It always runs in under a minute
items.explain: Idempotency: reruns are safe — same output, no double-counting. It is what makes backfills and retries sane.

items.q: A p-value of 0.03 means…
choices: If the null were true, you would see a result this extreme about 3% of the time
There is a 97% chance the alternative hypothesis is true
items.explain: A p-value is a statement about the data under the null, not about the probability the hypothesis is true — the single most-tested stats distinction.

items.q: In pandas, a left merge keeps…
choices: Every row from the left frame, with NaN where the right has no match
Only rows with matches on both sides
items.explain: Left join: all left rows survive; unmatched keys get NaN on the right's columns. Forgetting this silently drops data.

items.q: A metric improves overall but worsens within every user segment. This is…
choices: Simpson's paradox / confounding by segment mix
items.explain: Aggregates can reverse within-group trends when segment mix shifts — always slice before celebrating.

items.q: Randomization in an A/B test exists to…
choices: Balance known and unknown confounders across groups
items.explain: Random assignment is what lets you attribute the difference to the treatment rather than to who ended up in which group.

items.q: On a 99%-negative fraud dataset, 99% accuracy from an always-negative model tells you…
choices: Nothing useful — switch to precision/recall or PR-AUC
Accuracy is the right metric here
items.explain: Accuracy rewards the majority-class constant predictor. Imbalanced problems need precision/recall or PR curves.

items.q: Training accuracy keeps climbing while validation accuracy falls. This is…
choices: Overfitting: the model is memorizing noise
A data leak in the validation set
items.explain: The diverging curves are the textbook overfitting signature — time for regularization, simpler models, or more data.

items.q: Two variables are correlated. You may conclude…
choices: Nothing about causation without a design that isolates it
items.explain: Correlation is not causation, and the interview follow-up is always: what experiment or analysis would establish the causal link?

items.q: COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) differ when…
choices: Some rows have NULL emails — COUNT(column) skips NULLs
items.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. The difference is exactly the NULL count — a favorite screen question.

items.q: To find customers who placed no orders, you…
choices: LEFT JOIN orders and filter WHERE orders.id IS NULL
items.explain: The anti-join pattern: left join, then keep only rows where the right side is NULL — the 'who didn't' question.

items.q: Grouping daily revenue by month instead of by day changes…
choices: The grain of the analysis — and can hide or reveal trends
items.explain: Grain is an analytical choice: coarser grain smooths noise but can hide the very pattern the question is about.

items.q: A North Star metric is…
choices: The single metric that best captures the product's core value delivered
The metric with the biggest dashboard
items.explain: One metric tying product value to business outcomes, with input metrics feeding it — interviewers ask you to propose one for their product.

items.q: Cohort analysis groups users by…
choices: A shared characteristic or start period, then tracks them over time
items.explain: Cohorts (e.g., signup month) tracked over time separate real retention changes from mix shifts — the retention question's answer.

items.q: A bar chart with a truncated y-axis is…
choices: A dishonest exaggeration of small differences
items.explain: Starting bars above zero visually magnifies tiny gaps. Analyst interviews test whether you spot — and refuse — this.

items.q: Copying =A1*B1 down a column breaks when…
choices: B1 should have been an absolute reference ($B$1)
items.explain: Relative references shift on copy; lock the cell that must stay fixed with $. The classic spreadsheet-screen trap.

items.q: The bias-variance tradeoff says…
choices: Simpler models underfit (high bias); complex models overfit (high variance) — error is minimized between them
items.explain: Expected error decomposes into bias² + variance + noise. The interview follow-up is always: how do you find the sweet spot? (Validation.)

items.q: L1 regularization differs from L2 in that L1…
choices: Drives some weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection
items.explain: The L1 penalty's geometry creates sparsity — zero weights, i.e., automatic feature selection — where L2 merely shrinks.

items.q: k-fold cross-validation is used to…
choices: Estimate generalization while reducing the luck of a single split
items.explain: Averaging over folds gives a stabler performance estimate; every row serves as validation exactly once.

items.q: On heavily imbalanced data, ROC-AUC can be misleading because…
choices: It can stay high while precision on the rare class is terrible — use PR curves instead
It is undefined for binary problems
It requires balanced data to compute
items.explain: ROC-AUC's false-positive rate is diluted by the huge negative pool; precision-recall exposes rare-class performance.

items.q: A learning rate set far too high typically causes…
choices: Divergence or oscillation: the loss bounces or explodes instead of descending
items.explain: Overshooting the minimum each step is the signature of an excessive learning rate — the first thing to check when loss goes NaN.

items.q: Including 'days_until_churn_email_sent' as a feature to predict churn is…
choices: Leakage: the feature only exists after the outcome is known
items.explain: Leakage — information from the future masquerading as a feature — produces great validation scores and useless models.

items.q: You tune hyperparameters on the test set. The consequence is…
choices: An optimistic, invalid performance estimate — the test set is now a validation set
A better model with no downside
items.explain: Any decision made with test data contaminates it. Tune on validation, evaluate once on test — the discipline interviewers check.

items.q: WHERE and HAVING differ in that…
choices: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after
items.explain: Execution order: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING. Aggregate conditions belong in HAVING; row conditions in WHERE.

items.q: A window function differs from GROUP BY in that it…
choices: Returns a value per row while keeping row-level detail
items.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows; OVER() computes across rows but returns one value per row — ranking without losing detail.

items.q: A recursive CTE needs…
choices: An anchor member, a recursive member referencing the CTE, and UNION ALL between them
items.explain: Anchor seeds the result, the recursive member builds on it, UNION ALL combines — plus a termination condition or it never ends.

items.q: A self-join is the natural tool for…
choices: Comparing rows within one table, like employees to their managers
items.explain: Aliasing the same table twice lets rows relate to other rows — hierarchies, pairs, and period comparisons.

items.q: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC)…
choices: Splits the ordered rows into 4 roughly equal buckets
items.explain: NTILE divides the ordered set into N buckets — quartiles with NTILE(4), deciles with NTILE(10).

items.q: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) vs COUNT(user_id): use the first when…
choices: Duplicate user_ids would inflate the count and you need unique users
items.explain: Fan-out from joins is the classic cause: the same user counted once per joined row unless DISTINCT collapses them.

items.q: A correlated subquery…
choices: References the outer query and re-executes per outer row — often rewritable as a join
Is always faster than a join
items.explain: Correlation means per-row re-evaluation — correct but slow on big tables; EXISTS-to-join rewrites are the standard fix.
